query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Large-scale atomistic simulations of bulk HfNbTaTiZr with explicit 1 wt.% O defects will predict thermal conductivities in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes more accurately than existing analytical models restricted to defect-free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Fully dense, polycrystalline bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy containing 1 wt.% oxygen under ambient pressure.
generation.intervention: Implementation of atomistic or mesoscale simulations (e.g., molecular dynamics with ab initio-informed force fields) that treat randomly distributed O defects, lattice disorder, and temperature-dependent phonon scattering explicitly.
generation.conditions: Thermal conductivity measurements from near 0−200 K and 300−1200 K, performed in mildly oxidizing atmosphere or vacuum, matching known literature data ranges for HfNbTaTiZr specimens with 1 wt.% O.
generation.structural_mediator: Randomly dispersed oxygen interstitials and associated local lattice distortions, which scatter phonons across the entire temperature range.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly accounting for non-ideal defect structures, the simulations capture abnormal phonon scattering pathways that analytical approaches neglect, improving agreement with measured oxygen-containing specimens across cryogenic and high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Predicted thermal conductivity values in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K ranges will deviate from experimental data by lower than 10–15%, outperforming simpler continuum or perfect-crystal-based phenomenological models by at least a factor of two in accuracy.
generation.baseline: Prior continuum-based analytical models for perfect crystals that exclude oxygen defect content and typically exhibit errors exceeding 25% for real samples.
generation.boundary: Applicability is limited to HfNbTaTiZr alloys with ≤1 wt.% O over the 0–1200 K range. For heavily oxidized (>1 wt.% O) samples or temperatures beyond 1200 K, the approach’s parameterization becomes uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: If oxygen-vacancy clustering or secondary phase formation is significant, or if the local environment differs substantially from the assumed random defect distribution, the predicted conductivity may deviate beyond the stated accuracy range.

falsification_experiment.design: Obtain multiple specimens (with 1 wt.% O) confirmed by compositional analysis and measure their thermal conductivities via conventional methods (e.g., laser flash) from 10 K to 150 K and from 300 K to 1200 K under identical conditions used for model input data.
measurements: Measure oxygen content by gas analysis (e.g., carrier gas hot extraction).

Perform temperature-dependent thermal diffusivity measurements and calculate thermal conductivity using specific heat and density, focusing on both cryogenic (10–200 K) and elevated temperatures (300–1200 K).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured thermal conductivity in either the low- or high-temperature range deviates by more than 15% from the predicted values, the hypothesis that explicit defect-aware simulations significantly improve accuracy is invalidated.

cited_evidence.text: To gain additional insights into the phonon behaviour in equiatomic CoCrFeNiCu HEA, the mean phonon velocity v, phonon mean free path (MFP) lp, and lifetime of phonons τ at different temperatures were calculated. The mean phonon velocity, v, can be obtained from the slope of the 1/kp-1/lz fitting curve, lp can be obtained from the expression lp = 3kp/Cvv, and the mean phonon lifetime τ equals lp/v [,]. In Table 4, as the temperature increases from 300 K to 900 K, the phonon MFP is reduced by 46.5 %, the phonon velocity increases by 19.9 %. Such result shows that the phonon MFP is more sensitive to the temperature change. As the temperature increases, the atoms are accelerated and collisions are intensified. The accelerated thermal vibration of the lattice aggravates the lattice distortion [] and thus increases the probability of the lattice defects, causing the scattering of phonons and reducing the MFP of phonons. At 300K, the phonon MFPs of pure metals Cu, Co, and Ni are approximately 100, 70, and 85 Å, respectively [], which are much larger than the MFP of the equiatomic CoCrFeNiCu. This indicates that adding elements could significantly reduce the MFP of the alloy.

Figure 3 shows the temperature dependence of the measured κ, and the derived values of κe and κg for NiCoFeCrMn and NiCoFeCrPd. One distinct feature of the concentrated alloys, relative to pure metals, is that in a pure metal the total thermal conductivity is dominated by κe, and κg is usually negligible. However, in concentrated alloys, κg seems to dominate at low temperatures and is comparable with κe at about room temperature. Chemical disorder appears to scatter electrons more effectively than phonons. In addition, in pure metals κ starts decreasing at a few tens of K, while in concentrated alloys κ keeps increasing up to at least 300 K (see Table 3). One major reason is that, due to the large and nearly constant resistivity of these complex alloys, κe almost linearly increases with temperature up to 300 K, which is very different from the behavior in pure metals. The theoretical description of the temperature dependence of κg for disordered alloys has been challenging.
